sentences.text: The only known species, Elmisaurus rarus, lived approximately 70 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now Asia.

Because the fossils are incomplete, the animal's full appearance remains uncertain, though the holotype — the specimen the species is based on — is estimated to have reached a body length of 1.68 meters.
Like all oviraptorosaurs, this creature was a feathered, warm-blooded biped.
Its foot was light and slender, measuring about 15 centimeters in length.
The hand was roughly 20 centimeters long and slender, featuring bone shafts that were much narrower than the ends, a trait not seen in other oviraptorosaurs.
The claws on the hand were strongly curved.
A second specimen, the paratype ZPAL MgD-I/20, is one-fifth longer than the holotype.
The generic name means "foot sole" because the type specimen consisted of a metatarsus.
Elmisaurus rarus is the first discovered caenagnathid for which both hands and feet are known.
Fossil evidence suggests the forehead bones showed a high crest continuing through the nose.
Two fragmentary specimens of a small theropod were discovered in 1970 by a Polish-Mongolian expedition in the Ömnögovĭ province of Mongolia.
Elmisaurus rarus was discovered in 1970 and described in 1981 by Halszka Osmólska.
A 2001 study by Bruce Rothschild and colleagues examined 23 foot bones referred to Elmisaurus for stress fractures but found none.
The vertebrae were highly pneumatized.
The shoulder joint directed outward and downward.
The first finger was slender.
A bump on the top surface of the fourth metatarsal protruded over the fifth metatarsal bone and rose above the midfoot joint surface.
Elmisaurus was previously considered a relative of Chirostenotes within Elmisauridae and later Caenagnathidae, but this relationship was questioned by Maryanska et al. in 2002.
A 2013 analysis by Longrich et al. classified Elmisaurus as a caenagnathid.
A 2007 analysis by Senter places Elmisaurus with Chirostenotes and Hagryphus, distinct from Avimimus.
Elmisaurus lived from 72.2 to 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
In 1997, Hans-Dieter Sues argued that the second species should be referred to Chirostenotes, a view not accepted by Philip J. Currie.
While a relationship with Avimimus is possible, a 2007 analysis by Senter places Elmisaurus with Chirostenotes and Hagryphus, far from Avimimus.
